senses.gloss:
Rati
(‘[one who gives] enjoyment or pleasure’)
------------------------------------------
One of the specialities or peculiarities of हिन्दुइस्म् is that every aspect of life—good or not-so-good—is deified or has a presiding deity or spirit. If काम or desire in general and sexual love in particular has been deified as Kāmadeva (also known as Anaṅga, Madana and मन्मथ), his feminine counterpart or consort is रति.
The पुराणस् describe her as one of the daughters of दक्ष-प्रजापति and married to काम, son of another प्रजापति, called धर्म.
Prīti is her co-wife.
In sculptures and paintings she is shown in the company of काम or मन्मथ.
When sculptured independently she is shown as exceedingly beautiful, bedecked with several jewels and ornaments and in a dancing pose.
She may also be shown as riding a parrot, holding in her two hands the sugarcane stalk as the bow and five kinds of flower-darts.
Other objects shown in her hands are: vīṇā (lute), दण्ड (staff) and akṣasūtra (rosary).
According to the Bhāgavata (10.55) and the Viṣṇupurāṇa (5.27) she was reborn as Māyāvatī, a wife of the demon Śambara, but was reunited with her husband मन्मथ, now reborn as प्रद्युम्न, the son of कृष्ण and रुक्मिणी.
See also KĀMA and MANMATHA.

Rātrisūkta
(‘the hymn addressed to the [goddess] रात्रि’)
------------------------------------------
Sūktas are certain special groups of Vedic mantras. They may be used either for certain rites and rituals or as prayer.
The Rātrisūkta of the Ṛgveda (10.127.1-8) is one such well-known piece.
Though it has only eight ṛks or mantras, its use in rituals often includes 13 more verses called खिल or परिशिष्ट (additional) mantras which too are considered as of hoary antiquity. Then comes another group of 12 verses which are the phalaśruti (eulogy of the hymn itself that describes the various benefits one gets by reciting or using it).
A brief summary of this सूक्त may now be given:
As she arrives, Rātrī (the presiding goddess of the night) sees or observes every place through her beautiful and bright eyes (= the स्तर्स्). She, the immortal goddess, has filled the whole earth and the sky with darkness, enlivening it however, with the light of her स्तर्स्. After some time she departs, making way for her sister, उषस् (the dawn). Darkness too is withdrawn.
Even as the birds rest in their nests in the night, we too will safely spend the night in our houses. May she, the goddess of night, be pleased with us! Is it not a fact that as soon as night approaches, all people return to their homes, the cows and the horses to their sheds and the birds to their nests?
O goddess of the night, please accept this hymn of praise, like an oblation of ghee given in a sacrifice!
The 13 verses of the खिल section that follow, describe her form and beauty. They also contain prayers for protection against the dangers of wars, of enemies, of fire, of robbers and of the evil effects of malefic प्लनेत्स्.
The 12 verses that come next describe how to worship the goddess using these verses—by reciting them and offering milk and sandal-paste.
The results of this recitation and worship are also given. Some of them are: attaining fame in the three worlds; being blessed with a worthy son and wealth; a blind person regaining eyesight; a person suffering from diseases being cured of them; and, getting whatever one desires.
This Rātrisūkta is chanted as a part of the ceremonial recitation of the famous Caṇḍī or Durgāsaptaśatī also.

ratnapātra
(‘bowl of precious stones’)
------------------------------------------
The many deities described in the Hindu mythological works have provided Hindu इचोनोग्रफ्य् with plenty of material to describe and to work upon.
Apart from their dresses and ornaments, these deities hold several things in their hands. One of these is the ratna-pātra. It is actually a golden bowl (pātra) studded with ratnas or precious stones.
The deities in whose hands this is shown are: अन्नपूर्णा, कुबेर, and गणेश.
Annapūrṇā’s bowl is filled with ड़ोओद् whereas it is full of jewels in the hands of the other two deities.

Ratnaprabhā
------------------------------------------
The Brahmasūtras is the main and basic treatise on Vedānta philosophy. It is based entirely on the major उपनिषद्स्.
Being in the form of terse sūtras or laconic aphorisms, it cannot be understood without the help of a bhāṣya or a commentary. All the three ācāryas (teachers) of the major systems of Vedānta have written bhāṣyas on it, the one by शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) being the earliest.
On शङ्कर’s Brahmasūtrabhāṣya three subcommentaries, known generally as ṭīkās, are famous. They are Bhāmatī of वाचस्पति (9th century A. D.), Nyāya-nirṇaya of आनन्दगिरि (A. D. 1260) and Ratnaprabhā of रामानन्द (17th century A. D.).
The Ratnaprabhā is the simplest of the three and often contains the essence of the other two ṭīkās.
It is also called, sometimes, Bhāṣya-ratnaprabhā. If the bhāṣya of शङ्कर is the ratna or diamond, this ṭīkā is its prabhā or light, since it manifests that ‘light’ through its explanations.
See also BRAHMASŪTRAS.

Rātri
(‘One who gives [rest or happiness]’)
------------------------------------------
The benevolent goddess ruling over night, she is the sister of उषस् (dawn). She is of Ṛgvedic antiquity. She is described as wearing black robes studded with glittering स्तर्स्.
She is invoked for warding off the threat of darkness (like robbers, reptiles, wild animals and wicked spirits).
See also RĀTRISŪKTA.
